name: Belém Tower
label: Belém Tower
camera_source: Researched viewpoint 'Avenida de Brasília' (3 web pages); placed at the stretch of Avenida de Brasília nearest the subject (our map tiles).
pin_note: Position from OpenStreetMap way/24341353: the middle of the OpenStreetMap outline 'Tower of Belém' (52 m across).

text.description: Belém Tower is a small, ornate fortress standing at the edge of the Tagus, and it is one of the easiest buildings in Lisbon to photograph. It was finished in 1519 and built from local lioz limestone. It is made up of a low bastion and a four-storey tower about 30 metres high. The carved stonework, domed turrets and sculpted crosses give it plenty of detail, and the river behind it gives a clean, open background. It was built to guard the mouth of the river and to greet the ships of Portuguese explorers returning home, and today it is listed by UNESCO together with the nearby Jerónimos Monastery. One popular story says the tower once stood in the middle of the river. In fact it was built on a small island close to the shore. For the classic picture, use the riverside promenade north of the tower, which one guide lists as Avenida de Brasília. Standing there keeps most of the tourist clutter out of your frame and lets you include both the tower and the water. Late light gives the stonework a warm glow. It is also at its most photogenic at high tide, when water surrounds the bastion. If you have time, the lawns of Jardim da Torre de Belém give a second view, showing the full river-facing front framed by greenery. Take a few frames from each spot, because the angle changes the whole mood of the picture.
text.geographic_location: Belém Tower stands on the north bank of the Tagus in Belém, in the west of Lisbon, close to the Jerónimos Monastery. It sits at the water's edge, with a riverside promenade and gardens beside it.
text.directions_text: From the tram 15E stop at Largo da Princesa, the tower is about 6 minutes on foot to the south. From the Pedrouços stop (also tram 15E), it is about 9 minutes on foot to the south-east. The phone icon on the map is about 190 m north of the subject. The Navigate buttons below take you straight there.

shooting_on_your_phone.phone_lens: Start with the default lens (1x) for the tower and the river together. Switch to the ultra-wide (0.5x) if you want to include more sky and water or are standing close. Use the telephoto (2x-5x, depending on your phone) to pick out the turrets and carved crosses.
shooting_on_your_phone.where_to_stand: Stand about 190 m north of the subject, on Avenida de Brasília (the phone icon on the map), and face south. In late light the tower catches warm, low light. Walk to Jardim da Torre de Belém if you also want the tower's full river-facing front.
shooting_on_your_phone.how_to_frame: Turn on the gridlines and place the tower on one of the vertical lines, leaving open sky and water on the other side. Keep the horizon level. For a different version, go to Jardim da Torre de Belém and use the lawns and trees to frame the tower.
shooting_on_your_phone.phone_settings_tip: Tap on the tower to focus, then drag the exposure slider down a little in late light so the sky keeps its colour and the stonework does not wash out. In dim light after sunset, use night mode and hold the phone steady against a railing or your body.
shooting_on_your_phone.best_time: Late in the day, when low light gives the stonework a warm glow. The tower also looks best at high tide, when water surrounds the bastion.

text.access_note: The promenade and gardens are open public space, but going inside the tower may be ticketed or restricted, and the interior was reported closed for restoration, so check the official site before you go.

name: Jerónimos Monastery
label: Jerónimos Monastery
camera_source: Researched viewpoint 'Jardim da Praça do Império' (3 web pages); placed at OpenStreetMap 'Jardim da Praça do Império' (relation/9227991): middle (292 m across); moved 25 m off water.
pin_note: Position from OpenStreetMap way/974618750: the middle of the OpenStreetMap outline 'Monastery of the Hieronymites' (338 m across).

text.description:
The Jerónimos Monastery is a former monastery of the Order of Saint Jerome in Belém, close to the Tagus. It is one of the best-known examples of Manueline architecture in Lisbon, a richly carved style full of maritime detail. Building began on 6 January 1501 and took about a hundred years. The stone is a gold-coloured limestone, so the long south façade glows when the light is soft. Vasco da Gama's tomb is in the church nave, and the monastery has been a UNESCO World Heritage Site since 1983, together with the nearby Tower of Belém.

The classic photo is the whole façade in one frame from the far edge of the Jardim da Praça do Império. The phone icon on the map is there, looking towards the monastery. The gardens' central fountain or reflecting pools can sit in the foreground and give the picture depth. The building is very long, so leave a little space around it rather than cropping tight. If you want the carved detail, walk over to the Portal Sul for a close view of the south portal and its figures.

The site is very busy, so expect people in the foreground. Early morning or late afternoon gives softer light that suits the stone. Photos from inside the monastery are a separate matter: rules vary, so check them on arrival.
text.geographic_location: The monastery is in the Belém district of western Lisbon, beside the Tagus. It stands just north of the Jardim da Praça do Império gardens and not far from the Tower of Belém.
text.directions_text: Take tram 15E to the Mosteiro dos Jerónimos stop; the monastery is to the west, about 220 m away. The Centro Cultural de Belém stop (also tram 15E) is about 4 minutes away, with the monastery to the north-east of it. From either, walk to the gardens and go to their far edge, facing the monastery. The phone icon on the map is about 160 m south-east of the subject. The Navigate buttons below take you straight there.

shooting_on_your_phone.phone_lens: Start with the default lens (1x) for the whole façade. If you cannot fit it all in, switch to the ultra-wide (0.5x). Use telephoto (2x-5x) for carved details and the tops of the towers.
shooting_on_your_phone.where_to_stand: Stand about 160 m south-east of the subject, in Jardim da Praça do Império (the phone icon on the map), and face north-west. From here the full length of the south façade fits in one frame, often with the central fountain or reflecting pools in front.
shooting_on_your_phone.how_to_frame: Switch on gridlines and line the horizontal ledges of the building up with them so the façade does not lean. Keep the phone level and use the water or fountain as a foreground. For a closer view of the carved portal and its figures, Portal Sul is a good second spot.
shooting_on_your_phone.phone_settings_tip: Tap the stone façade to focus, then slide the exposure down a little if the sky is bright, so the gold limestone keeps its colour. When you zoom in on the carvings, hold the phone steady with both hands, braced against your body.
shooting_on_your_phone.best_time: Early morning or late afternoon, when the light is softer.

text.access_note: The gardens and the outside views are open public space, but the monastery interior is a ticketed site with its own photography rules, so check the official site before you go.
claims_not_in_sources: Soft light makes the gold-coloured limestone look warmer in early morning or late afternoon.
Still water in the reflecting pools can show a reflection of the façade.
Walking time from the Centro Cultural de Belém tram stop is about 4 minutes.

name: São Jorge Castle
label: São Jorge Castle
camera_source: Researched viewpoint 'Miradouro de São Pedro de Alcântara' (3 web pages); placed at OpenStreetMap 'Miradouro de São Pedro de Alcântara' (node/419313189): point.
pin_note: Position from OpenStreetMap way/1382432568: the middle of the OpenStreetMap outline 'São Jorge Castle' (113 m across).

text.description: São Jorge Castle sits on a hill above the old centre, and from across the valley it reads as a long line of pale walls and towers above the rooftops of the Baixa. That is why it photographs so well from outside: the hill gives the castle a natural frame, and the old town fills the middle of the picture. People have lived on this hill since at least the 8th century BC, and the oldest fortifications date from the 2nd century BC. The Portuguese took the castle in 1147, and it was later dedicated to Saint George under King John I. It was also a royal palace, and Vasco da Gama was received here in 1498. Today it is a national monument and museum. For this shot, use the phone icon on the map: the Miradouro de São Pedro de Alcântara. It gives a side view across the valley to the castle hill. The tiled map on the terrace helps you name the buildings you are photographing. The castle's own walls and esplanade are the best place for views of the city, but they are behind a ticket. The viewpoints around the castle are free, so you can still get a strong picture without going in. Keep the castle on a third of the frame and let the rooftops fill the rest.
text.geographic_location: The castle is on the hill above the Baixa and the Alfama rooftops, in the Santa Maria Maior district of central Lisbon.
text.directions_text: From Rossio (Metro Green line) the castle hill is about 385 m to the east; from Martim Moniz (Metro Green line, tram 12E, tram 28E) it is about 308 m to the south-east. The tram 12E stops at Rua dos Lagares and Largo do Terreirinho are close to the hill too. The viewpoint is easy to reach on foot from Bairro Alto, and from there the castle is about 930 m to the east. The phone icon on the map is about 890 m west of the subject. The Navigate buttons below take you straight there.

shooting_on_your_phone.phone_lens: Start with the default lens (1x) for the whole scene. Then try telephoto (2x-3x, or up to 5x if your phone has it) to pick out the castle walls across the valley.
shooting_on_your_phone.where_to_stand: Stand about 890 m west of the subject, on Miradouro de São Pedro de Alcântara (the phone icon on the map), and face east. From the terrace you see the castle hill from the side, with the Baixa and old town rooftops in the middle ground.
shooting_on_your_phone.how_to_frame: Turn on the gridlines and put the castle on one of the upper thirds, with rooftops filling the lower part. Use the default lens (1x) for the full valley and 2x or more to isolate the walls. For a different angle, the Miradouro da Senhora do Monte gets you much closer to the castle, roughly level with its walls.
shooting_on_your_phone.phone_settings_tip: Tap the castle to focus, then slide the exposure down a little so the pale walls and sky do not wash out. Hold the phone steady against the railing for the zoomed shots.
shooting_on_your_phone.best_time: Check the light on the day. The sun is in the west in the afternoon, so it will be behind you when you look east towards the castle.

text.access_note: The viewpoint is a free public terrace; the castle itself is a ticketed site, so check the official site before you go.
claims_not_in_sources: The sun is in the west in the afternoon, so it is behind you when you look east from the viewpoint.
Pale walls can look washed out against a bright sky, so lowering the exposure a little helps.

name: Alfama
label: Alfama
camera_source: Researched viewpoint 'Miradouro das Portas do Sol' (4 web pages); placed at OpenStreetMap 'Miradouro das Portas do Sol' (way/565894105): middle (41 m across).
pin_note: Position from OpenStreetMap node/207597971: the OpenStreetMap point 'Alfama'.

text.description: Alfama is the oldest neighbourhood in Lisbon, spread over the slope between São Jorge Castle and the River Tagus. Its name comes from an Arabic word for hot springs. The 1755 earthquake did not destroy it, so it is still a tangle of narrow lanes and small squares. That is why it photographs so well. From Miradouro das Portas do Sol you look down on red-tiled rooftops stepping toward the river, with the towers of São Vicente de Fora and the dome of the National Pantheon (the former Church of Santa Engrácia) in the skyline. The terrace has a statue of São Vicente, which gives wide shots a clear focal point. Most of what makes Alfama special is down in the lanes, but this terrace gives you the whole picture in one frame. Take a wide photo of the rooftops and river first. Then zoom in on the towers, the dome or a patch of tiles. Stand at the eastern edge of the terrace, toward the river, to get the river and roofs together with the monuments behind. If the terrace is busy, Miradouro de Santa Luzia is also in Alfama. It has a bougainvillea-covered pergola and blue-and-white tile panels on the church wall, with the same rooftops falling away behind. Crowds there vary too, and it is quiet mainly at sunrise or after about 17:00.
text.geographic_location: Alfama lies in central Lisbon on the hillside below São Jorge Castle, running down toward the Tagus. The terrace is on its upper side, with the old rooftops spread out to the east of it.
text.directions_text: From Santa Apolónia (Metro Blue line), head south-west up into Alfama; it is about 556 m on foot. From Terreiro do Paço (Metro Blue line), head north-east; it is about 741 m on foot. The easiest way is tram 28E to Rua das Escolas Gerais (about 177 m on foot, heading south-east) or Calçada de São Vicente (about 193 m on foot, heading south). The phone icon on the map is about 140 m west of the subject. The Navigate buttons below take you straight there.

shooting_on_your_phone.phone_lens: Start with the default lens (1x) for the main view. Switch to ultra-wide (0.5x) if you want more river and sky. Use telephoto (2x-5x, depending on your phone) to pick out the São Vicente de Fora towers and the Pantheon dome.
shooting_on_your_phone.where_to_stand: Stand about 140 m west of the subject, on Miradouro das Portas do Sol (the phone icon on the map), and face east. At the eastern edge of the terrace toward the river. From here the stepped red rooftops fall away toward the Tagus, with the towers and dome in the skyline. The old streets of Alfama lie just to the east of you.
shooting_on_your_phone.how_to_frame: Put the rooftops in the lower two-thirds and the river in the upper third, and use the gridlines to keep the horizon level. Use the São Vicente statue as a foreground focal point for a wide shot. Then take a second, zoomed photo of the towers and dome. As an alternative viewpoint, Miradouro de Santa Luzia, also in Alfama, has a pergola and blue-and-white tiles, though crowds there vary.
shooting_on_your_phone.phone_settings_tip: Tap the rooftops to focus, then slide the exposure down a little so the sky keeps its colour and the tiles stay rich. Try panorama mode for the full sweep down to the river, and move slowly and steadily.
shooting_on_your_phone.best_time: Early morning, or late afternoon before the terrace fills up. Weekday mornings before 10:30 are suggested, and in summer it is best to avoid the middle of the day, roughly 11:00 to 16:00.

text.access_note: Miradouro das Portas do Sol is an open public terrace that is free to reach on foot or by tram 28E; opening and crowd levels can vary, so check the official site before you go.
claims_not_in_sources: The streets from the Metro stations up into Alfama are uphill, so the walking distances given may feel longer than they sound.
Keeping the horizon level using gridlines and lowering exposure will help keep sky colour and tile detail in a bright rooftop view.

name: LX Factory
label: LX Factory
camera_source: Researched viewpoint 'Livraria Ler Devagar' (3 web pages); placed at our map tiles: 'Ler Devagar' (pois); moved 5 m off buildings.
pin_note: Position from OpenStreetMap way/221960606: kept: no OpenStreetMap object carries this Wikidata ID.

text.description: LX Factory is a former industrial complex with shops, where old brick and steel factory buildings sit under the huge 25 de Abril Bridge. It photographs well because of the contrast: rough industrial walls, street art, and the huge bridge overhead. The most photographed corner is inside Livraria Ler Devagar, a bookshop in a former printing hall. Here the bookshelves run from floor to ceiling, metal walkways cross the space, and a white bicycle hangs in the air above you. Stand on the ground floor and point your phone upwards to get all of that in one frame. The bookshop is still a working shop with customers browsing, so keep your phone use quiet and avoid pointing it at people. If you want an outdoor view as well, the lanes of LX Factory show the brick and steel buildings with the bridge towering behind and street art on the walls. The exact angle for the bridge is easiest to find on site, so walk around a little. Photography for commercial work is restricted here, as it is a managed commercial area. Drones are restricted too. The Sunday flea market is the busiest time, which makes clear shots harder.
text.geographic_location: LX Factory is right beside the 25 de Abril Bridge. It is a short walk from Estação de Santo Amaro (tram 15E).
text.directions_text: Take tram 15E to Estação de Santo Amaro, then walk about 170 m; LX Factory is to the east of the stop. Alternatively, take tram 18E to Rua Leão de Oliveira, about 240 m on foot, with the complex to the south. The phone icon on the map is about 20 m north-east of the numbered pin. The Navigate buttons below take you straight there.

shooting_on_your_phone.phone_lens: Start with the ultra-wide (0.5x) inside the bookshop so you can fit the tall shelves, the walkways and the hanging bicycle into one frame. Switch to the default lens (1x) for a calmer, less stretched view of a single section. Outside, the ultra-wide helps with the bridge above the buildings, and the telephoto (2x-5x) is good for street-art details.
shooting_on_your_phone.where_to_stand: Stand about 20 m north-east of the numbered pin, at the phone icon on the map, and face south-west. Livraria Ler Devagar is inside the complex: stand inside on the ground floor and look up at the tall shelves and the suspended white bicycle, framed by the metal walkways of the former printing hall.
shooting_on_your_phone.how_to_frame: Switch on the gridlines and keep the phone upright, so the shelves stay as straight as you can manage. Place the bicycle on one of the upper grid intersections and let the shelves and walkways fill the rest of the frame. For an outdoor alternative, walk back into the LX Factory lanes and frame the brick and steel buildings with the bridge above them.
shooting_on_your_phone.phone_settings_tip: Tap the bicycle to focus, then slide the exposure down a little if bright lights wash out the shelves. If the shop is dim, hold the phone steady against a shelf or your body when using night mode, and be discreet with customers around you.
shooting_on_your_phone.best_time: The Sunday flea market is the busiest time, so a quieter day is easier for clean shots indoors and out.

text.access_note: LX Factory is a managed commercial area with shops and a working bookshop, and commercial photography and drones are restricted, so check the official site before you go.

name: Rossio
label: Rossio
camera_source: Researched viewpoint 'Miradouro de São Pedro de Alcântara' (1 web pages); placed at OpenStreetMap 'Miradouro de São Pedro de Alcântara' (node/419313189): point.
pin_note: Position from OpenStreetMap way/1317749306: 'Dom Pedro IV', the best-known feature inside 'Dom Pedro IV Square' (262 m across).

text.description:
Rossio is the popular name for Praça de D. Pedro IV, one of Lisbon's main squares since the Middle Ages and still a favourite meeting place for locals and visitors. Its name is roughly 'commons', from the days when it was an open market ground. Most of what you see was rebuilt after the great 1755 earthquake, which gives the buildings around the square their even, Pombaline look. The Column of Pedro IV stands in the middle and dates from 1874. The wave-patterned paving was laid in the 19th century, and the bronze fountains came from France. On the north-west side, the neo-Manueline front of the Rossio railway station is worth including, and the National Theatre D. Maria II closes the square at the north end.

The square is about 262 m across, so it is hard to fit into one frame from ground level. That is why this spot sends you to Miradouro de São Pedro de Alcântara, a free terrace with an elevated view down over Rossio towards the hilltop castle. From there you get the whole square, the rooftops and the hill beyond in one picture, away from the crowds crossing the paving. If you also want a close-up, go down to the square for the wave paving leading towards the column, or look through the yellow Arco da Bandeira gateway, which frames the whole square.
text.geographic_location: Rossio sits in the Pombaline Downtown (Baixa) of Lisbon, between the Restauradores area and Praça da Figueira. The viewpoint is on the slope to the north-west of the square, looking back down at it.
text.directions_text: Take the Metro Green line to Rossio station, a short walk from the square, or the Metro Blue line to Restauradores. Trams 12E, 15E and 25E stop at Praça da Figueira, close to the square. The phone icon on the map is about 450 m north-west of the subject. The Navigate buttons below take you straight there.

shooting_on_your_phone.phone_lens: Start with the default lens (1x) to take in the whole square and the castle hill. Switch to telephoto (2x-3x) to pick out the column, the fountains and the castle on the skyline. Use the ultra-wide (0.5x) when you go down into the square for the wave paving.
shooting_on_your_phone.where_to_stand: Stand about 450 m north-west of the subject, on Miradouro de São Pedro de Alcântara (the phone icon on the map), and face south-east. From here the square lies to the south-east, below you, with the hilltop castle beyond it. Keep the terrace railing or wall out of the bottom of the frame, or use it deliberately as a foreground edge.
shooting_on_your_phone.how_to_frame: Turn on the gridlines and put the horizon on the upper third line, so the square and rooftops fill most of the picture and the castle sits near the top. For a second picture, go to the square and shoot along the wave paving towards the column. Another option is to stand by the Arco da Bandeira and frame the square through the yellow arch.
shooting_on_your_phone.phone_settings_tip: Tap on the column or the castle to set focus, then drag the exposure slider down a little so the evening sky keeps its colour. After dark, use night mode and rest your elbows on the terrace wall to keep the phone still.
shooting_on_your_phone.best_time: Evening, when the city lights come on and the square and castle hill are lit.

text.access_note: The viewpoint is an open public terrace with no entry charge listed, and photography for personal use is generally fine in the square, but check the official site before you go if you plan anything beyond casual photos.
claims_not_in_sources: Miradouro de São Pedro de Alcântara is on the slope to the north-west of the square, above it (inferred from the map positions and the elevated view).
A telephoto lens makes the castle look closer and larger in the frame.
Placing the horizon on the upper gridline keeps the square and rooftops dominant in the frame.
The square is busy with people crossing it during the day.

name: Miradouro de Santa Luzia
label: Santa Luzia
camera_source: No separate stand-here point: photographed at the spot itself (indoors, from its top, or right in front of it); drawn as the split pin.

text.description: Miradouro de Santa Luzia is a small viewpoint terrace in the old part of Lisbon, looking out over the rooftops towards the river. It is a good place for a phone photo because the view is layered. Terracotta roofs sit in the foreground, the water lies beyond, and the sky fills the top of the frame. You don't need to climb or hunt for an angle, as the terrace itself is the vantage point. The phone icon on the map is at the viewpoint itself, so you can take your photo without walking further. A tram stop of the same name is about a minute away on foot, so the tram rattling past can also make a nice moment in a wider shot. For a first photo, use the default lens (1x) and turn on gridlines so the horizon sits level. Then step slightly left or right until the rooftops fill the lower third of the frame and the sky takes the rest. Use the ultra-wide (0.5x) lens if you want the whole terrace and its surroundings in one shot. Use 2x or more to pick out a single church dome or a patch of tiles on a roof. Keep an eye on other visitors, as the terrace is not large. Wait a few seconds for a clear gap rather than cropping people out afterwards. Wipe your lens before you start, because a smudge shows up clearly against bright sky.
text.geographic_location: In Lisbon's old riverside district, on a terrace above the rooftops, close to the Largo das Portas do Sol tram stop. It is about 640 m north-east of Terreiro do Paço station.
text.directions_text: The nearest stop is the tram stop Miradouro de Santa Luzia (tram 12E and tram 28E), about 1 minute on foot. Largo das Portas do Sol (also tram 12E and tram 28E) is a similar distance away. From Terreiro do Paço (Metro Blue line) it is about 10 minutes on foot, heading north-east. From Martim Moniz (Metro Green line, tram 12E, tram 28E) it is about 11 minutes on foot. The phone icon on the map is at the subject itself. The Navigate buttons below take you straight there.

shooting_on_your_phone.phone_lens: Start with the default lens (1x) for a natural view of rooftops and river. Switch to the ultra-wide (0.5x) to include more of the terrace and sky. Use the telephoto (2x-5x, depending on your phone) to pick out details such as a dome or a tower.
shooting_on_your_phone.where_to_stand: Stand right at the subject: the phone icon on the map marks the spot. Take your photos from the terrace edge, where the view over the rooftops is clearest.
shooting_on_your_phone.how_to_frame: Turn on gridlines and place the horizon on the upper or lower line instead of the middle. Keep the rooftops in the lower third if you want sky, or lower the phone slightly to give more space to the roofs and river. Include a bit of the terrace, such as a railing or a plant, in the foreground for depth.
shooting_on_your_phone.phone_settings_tip: Tap on the rooftops to set focus, then drag the exposure slider down a little so the sky keeps its colour. Try a Live Photo if a tram or a bird passes through the view.
shooting_on_your_phone.best_time: Late afternoon or early evening usually gives softer, warmer light on the rooftops. Early morning is likely to be quieter.

text.access_note: This is a viewpoint terrace, but check the official site before you go in case of any restrictions or works.
claims_not_in_sources: Miradouro de Santa Luzia is a viewpoint terrace with views over rooftops towards the river.
The terrace is fairly small and can get busy with visitors.
Late afternoon and early evening usually give softer, warmer light, and early morning is usually quieter.
Trams passing near the viewpoint can make a good addition to wider shots.

name: Bairro Alto
label: Bairro Alto
camera_source: Researched viewpoint 'Miradouro de São Pedro de Alcântara' (3 web pages); placed at OpenStreetMap '64 - Miradouro de S. Pedro de Alcântara' (node/12334692206): point.
pin_note: Position from OpenStreetMap way/945072679: large area 'Bairro Alto' (758 m across): previous pin kept, it lies inside.

text.description:
Bairro Alto means "Upper District" and is a central district of Lisbon. The best way to photograph it with a phone is to look at it from the edge, together with the city beyond. The district grew in the 16th century outside the old city walls, on a near-grid of straight streets and lanes. Its houses are mostly tall, narrow buildings of three to four storeys, with rows of windows and matching rooflines. It was not significantly affected by the 1755 earthquake.

The classic postcard view is from the Miradouro de São Pedro de Alcântara, a landscaped garden terrace at the edge of the district, next to the top of the Glória funicular. From here you look across the valley to São Jorge Castle and the Baixa, with the edge of Bairro Alto in the foreground. The kiosk, the tiled map and the sculpted garden give you something close to the lens, and the balustrade makes a handy frame. Keep the horizon level and let the foreground fill the bottom third of the picture.

This viewpoint shows the district from outside rather than its own streets. If you want a different angle, the Miradouro de Santa Catarina looks towards the river and the 25 de Abril Bridge. The top of the Elevador de Santa Justa gives a higher view over the Baixa, with Bairro Alto's rooftops close below.
text.geographic_location: Bairro Alto is a central district of Lisbon. São Pedro de Alcântara and Príncipe Real mark its northern edge, and the terrace sits right beside the top of the Glória funicular.
text.directions_text: The easiest start is the Glória funicular: get off at Glória - São Pedro de Alcântara, and the terrace is right beside the top station. From the phone icon on the map to the middle of the district is about 5 minutes on foot, heading south. Tram 24E stops at Largo Trindade Coelho and tram 28E at Calhariz (Bica), each about 3 minutes on foot from the middle of the district. The Bica funicular's Bica - Largo do Calhariz stop is also about 3 minutes on foot from the middle of the district. The phone icon on the map is about 330 m north of the subject. The Navigate buttons below take you straight there.

shooting_on_your_phone.phone_lens: Start with the default lens (1x) for the whole view of castle, valley and foreground. name: Lisbon Cathedral
label: Lisbon Cathedral
camera_source: Researched viewpoint 'Rua de Augusto Rosa' (3 web pages); placed at OpenStreetMap 'Rua Augusto Rosa' (way/49695163): point nearest the subject (171 m long).
pin_note: Position from OpenStreetMap relation/19372558: the middle of the OpenStreetMap outline 'Lisbon Cathedral' (135 m across).

text.description:
Lisbon Cathedral, known locally as the Sé, is the oldest church in the city, begun in 1147 after the city was reconquered from the Moors. It has been damaged by several earthquakes, notably the great one of 1755, and rebuilt and restored many times, so it mixes styles. From the street, though, you see the Romanesque west front, which looks more like a fortress than a church: two sturdy towers either side of the doorway, crenellations along the top and a rose window above the portal. It has been a National Monument since 1910.

It photographs well because the plain, weathered stone makes a strong backdrop, and the yellow tram 28E rattles right past the front. The classic picture is the tram passing in front of the facade, taken from the street rather than from inside the tram. The trams only come every 10 to 15 minutes, so be ready to wait a little, and keep an eye on pedestrians, tuk-tuks and cars crossing your frame.

Take a few test shots while you wait, then shoot as the tram enters the frame. If the street is too crowded, try Largo da Sé for the tram coming round the bend below the cathedral. For a different view, Rua da Saudade shows the cathedral's edge with the 25 de Abril Bridge behind it, though check the framing when you arrive.
text.geographic_location: In the Sé area of old Lisbon, with tram 28E running right past the front of the cathedral.
text.directions_text: The nearest Metro is Terreiro do Paço on the Metro Blue line, about 6 minutes on foot, with the cathedral to the north-east. Tram 28E and tram 12E stop at Limoeiro (about 1 minute on foot) and at Sé (about 2 minutes on foot). From Rossio on the Metro Green line it is about 10 minutes on foot to the south-east. Once there, find Rua de Augusto Rosa and follow the phone icon on the map. The phone icon on the map is at the subject itself. The Navigate buttons below take you straight there.

shooting_on_your_phone.phone_lens: Start with the default lens (1x) for the tram passing in front of the facade. Switch to the ultra-wide (0.5x) if the pavement is tight and you can't fit both towers in. Use telephoto (2x-5x, depending on your phone) for details like the rose window, or for the bridge-behind-the-cathedral view from Rua da Saudade.
shooting_on_your_phone.where_to_stand: Stand on Rua de Augusto Rosa, right in front of the subject: the phone icon on the map marks the spot. From here you see tram 28E passing in front of the Romanesque west front, with the stone towers behind it as a backdrop. Check the facade is in view before the tram arrives.
shooting_on_your_phone.how_to_frame: Turn on gridlines and keep the towers upright and the horizon level so the stone front looks solid. Place the tram's path along the lower third of the frame so the facade fills the space above it. Wait for the tram to line up with the doorway. If the street is busy, try Largo da Sé for the tram rounding the bend below the cathedral instead.
shooting_on_your_phone.phone_settings_tip: Tap on the facade to focus, then slide the exposure down a little so the bright sky doesn't wash out the stone. Try Live Photos or take several shots in a row as the tram passes, then pick the best frame.
shooting_on_your_phone.best_time: Morning, before about 9 am, when the street is emptier and the light from the east falls on the tram and facade.

text.access_note: The exterior and the street are open to everyone. Check the official site for opening hours and any entry rules before you go.

text.description:
Pink Street is the nickname for Rua Nova do Carvalho, a short pedestrian-feeling lane in the Cais do Sodré area. Its pavement is painted pink, and coloured umbrellas hang overhead. The street runs away toward a yellow bridge, framed by bar fronts. That mix of colours makes it easy to photograph on a phone, because the pink, the canopy and the bridge already form a strong picture.

The phone icon on the map is a short way east of the pink street, so you look west toward it. For an overhead view, there is a nearby alternative: the bridge that carries Rua do Alecrim over the street. Check the exact point on the map before you head up. From the bridge you look down on the pink surface and the umbrellas. Few people bother to climb up, so it is a different angle from the usual shots. You reach the bridge by walking around the block rather than straight from the street below.

If you also want the classic view, go down to Rua Nova do Carvalho itself. From there the whole pink pavement runs toward the yellow bridge, framed by the bar fronts and the umbrella canopy. The umbrella display changes over time, so the canopy may not match older photos you have seen. The street gets very busy from late morning and again at night, when it turns into a bar strip. For a clear view of the pavement, aim for a quieter hour.
text.geographic_location: Pink Street is in the Cais do Sodré area of central Lisbon, a few minutes' walk from the Cais do Sodré station. It is just below Rua do Alecrim, which crosses it on a bridge.
text.directions_text: From Cais do Sodré (Metro Green line, trams 15E and 18E), walk north-east; the street is about 3 minutes on foot. If you arrive by tram 25E, get off at Rua de São Paulo, about 1 minute on foot to the south-east of the street. From tram 28E, the Rua Vítor Cordon stop is about 2 minutes on foot to the south-west. For the overhead alternative, walk around the block to Rua do Alecrim and onto the bridge, which takes a little longer. The phone icon on the map is at the subject itself. The Navigate buttons below take you straight there.

shooting_on_your_phone.phone_lens: Start with the ultra-wide (0.5x) so the pink pavement and the umbrellas both fit in the frame, whether you shoot from where you stand or the overhead bridge. shooting_on_your_phone.where_to_stand: Stand on Rua do Alecrim, right in front of the subject: the phone icon on the map marks the spot. For an overhead view, walk around the block to the Rua do Alecrim bridge, which carries the road over Rua Nova do Carvalho, and check the exact point on the map. From the bridge you look down on the pink street and its umbrellas. For the ground-level alternative, stand on Rua Nova do Carvalho and look toward the yellow bridge.
shooting_on_your_phone.how_to_frame: Turn on the gridlines and line the street up with a vertical grid line so it runs through the picture. If you use the bridge, lean over the edge only as far as is safe and hold the phone with both hands. Include a strip of umbrellas at the top or edge to show the canopy. For the ground-level alternative, let the bar fronts and umbrellas frame the pink pavement leading to the yellow bridge.
shooting_on_your_phone.phone_settings_tip: Tap to focus on the pink pavement, then lower the exposure slider a little so the pink stays rich and the sky does not wash out. If the street is crowded, a Live Photo lets you choose a frame with fewer people in it.
shooting_on_your_phone.best_time: Early in the day is likely to be calmest, as the street gets heavy crowds from late morning and again at night, when it becomes a bar strip. At night, try night mode and brace your elbows against your body or a solid surface to keep the phone steady.

text.access_note: This is an open public street; check locally for any event or closure before you go.

text.description: The Santa Justa Lift is a slim wrought-iron tower standing at the end of Rua de Santa Justa in the Baixa. It links the lower streets with Largo do Carmo above. It is 45 metres tall, covers seven storeys and has a lookout on top. Engineer Raoul Mesnier du Ponsard drove the project. The metal structure was inaugurated in August 1901, and the first lift car ran in July 1902. It is the only conventional vertical lift left among Lisbon's urban lifts, and it was classified as a National Monument in 2002. It photographs well because the ironwork is full of fine detail, and it rises between the plainer Baixa buildings. The best phone picture here is a close upward view of the lacework from the foot of the tower. For a wider shot, Rua de Santa Justa shows the whole tower framed between the building fronts. Terraços do Carmo shows it from above, over the Baixa roofs. Please note that the lift itself may be temporarily closed, with no confirmed reopening date. Check carris.pt before going. The street-level view costs nothing, and early morning is the quietest time to stand and look up.
text.geographic_location: In the Baixa, in the Santa Maria Maior parish of central Lisbon. It stands at the end of Rua de Santa Justa, between the lower town and Largo do Carmo.
text.directions_text: From Baixa-Chiado (Metro Blue line and Green line) the lift is about 3 minutes on foot to the north. From Rossio (Metro Green line) it is about 4 minutes on foot to the south-west. If you come by tram 12E, 15E or 25E, get off at Figueira Square or Praça da Figueira. The lift is then about 3 minutes on foot to the south-west. The phone icon on the map is about 190 m south of the subject. The Navigate buttons below take you straight there.

shooting_on_your_phone.phone_lens: Walk from where you stand to the base of the tower first, then use the ultra-wide (0.5x) from the foot of the tower to fit the height of the ironwork into the frame. Switch to the telephoto (2x-5x, depending on your phone) to pick out the lacework and the details at the top.
shooting_on_your_phone.where_to_stand: Stand about 190 m south of the subject, on Rua do Ouro (the phone icon on the map), and face north. From there you can see the tower from a distance. For the close upward view, walk north to the base of the tower and look straight up the ironwork. You get a close view of the lacework and the structure rising above the street.
shooting_on_your_phone.how_to_frame: Turn on the gridlines and tilt the phone upwards, keeping the tower's centre line on the middle gridline so the frame feels balanced. For a different view, try Rua de Santa Justa for the whole tower between the building fronts, or Terraços do Carmo for the tower seen from above.
shooting_on_your_phone.phone_settings_tip: Tap the brightest part of the sky to set focus. Then slide the exposure down a little so the iron stays dark and detailed instead of washing out against the sky.
shooting_on_your_phone.best_time: Early morning, when it is quietest.

text.access_note: The view from the street is on a public street and costs nothing, but the lift itself is run by Carris and may be temporarily closed, so check carris.pt before you go.

name: Monument to the Discoveries
label: Padrão
camera_source: Researched viewpoint 'Avenida Brasília' (2 web pages); placed at OpenStreetMap 'Avenida de Brasília' (way/429797068): point nearest the subject (517 m long).
pin_note: Position from OpenStreetMap way/152327819: the middle of the OpenStreetMap outline 'Monument to the Discoveries' (50 m across).

text.description:
The Monument to the Discoveries (Padrão dos Descobrimentos) stands on the north bank of the Tagus at Belém. It is shaped like the prow of a caravel, the kind of ship used in early Portuguese exploration, and it rises 56 metres beside the water. Henry the Navigator stands at the front. Along the two ramps behind him are 33 figures in all, including monarchs, explorers, cartographers and missionaries. All of them lean forward towards the sea.

It photographs well because the shape is so clear. The prow and the figures make a strong outline against the sky, and the river sits behind it. The present monument was built between 1958 and 1960 and opened on 9 August 1960, to mark five centuries since Henry's death. In front of it, a 50-metre compass-rose pavement includes a world map 14 metres wide.

For a simple shot, use the riverside walkway on Avenida Brasília and look up at the prow with the figures visible. If you want the whole monument with the compass rose below it, walk back onto the paved square (the Rosa dos Ventos). The view from the top, reached by lift or 267 stairs, takes in the river, Belém Tower and the Jerónimos Monastery. Queues can be long and tour groups gather at the popular spots, so allow some patience and be ready to wait for a clear frame.
text.geographic_location: It is in Belém, in the civil parish of Santa Maria de Belém, on the north bank of the Tagus beside Belém Marina. The Praça do Império, the Jerónimos Monastery and the Belém Cultural Centre lie across the main road from it.
text.directions_text: From the Mosteiro dos Jerónimos stop on tram 15E, the monument is to the south, about 430 m on foot. The Centro Cultural de Belém stop, also on tram 15E, is about the same distance away, with the monument to the south-east. Head towards the river, crossing the wide road that separates the gardens from the waterfront. The monument is the tall rose-tinted stone prow by the water. The phone icon on the map is about 680 m north-east of the subject. The Navigate buttons below take you straight there.

shooting_on_your_phone.phone_lens: Start with the default lens (1x) from the walkway to get the prow and the sky together. Switch to ultra-wide (0.5x) if you stand close or want the compass-rose pavement in the foreground. Use telephoto (2x-5x, depending on your phone) to pick out Henry the Navigator and the figures along the ramps.
shooting_on_your_phone.where_to_stand: Stand about 680 m north-east of the subject, on Avenida Brasília (the phone icon on the map), and face south-west. From here you get a distant view of the whole monument. For the close view, looking up at the caravel prow with the figures visible, go to the riverside walkway on Avenida Brasília nearer the monument; that position is approximate.
shooting_on_your_phone.how_to_frame: Turn on gridlines and keep the monument's edge near a vertical line. Hold the phone level, because tilting it upwards makes the walls lean inwards. Leave a little sky above the prow. For a second angle, walk onto the Rosa dos Ventos square to include the monument's full height with the compass-rose mosaic in front.
shooting_on_your_phone.phone_settings_tip: Tap on the stonework to set focus, then slide the exposure down a little so the pale stone keeps its detail against a bright sky. If you take a Live Photo, hold still for a moment after pressing the button.
shooting_on_your_phone.best_time: The walkway can be busy with tour groups, so allow some patience for a clear frame.

text.access_note: The riverside walkway and the square are open public space, but going inside or up to the top is ticketed, so check the official site before you go for prices and opening hours.

text.description: Tram 28E threading through Alfama makes a memorable photo, and one of the most famous tram photo locations is Rua das Escolas Gerais. The street bends tightly between pastel-coloured houses, and the church of São Vicente de Fora rises above the rooftops. When the tram rounds the corner, you get the narrow lane, the colour and the old neighbourhood in one frame. The lane fits only one vehicle at a time, so the tram fills the gap between the walls and looks properly close and chunky on a phone screen. Stand at the tight bend, ideally at the crossroads with Calçada de São Vicente, and let the tram come to you. You may need patience: wait for a clear moment, then shoot as the tram turns. If you want a second angle, Largo das Portas do Sol shows the tram passing the statue of Saint Vincent with the dome of São Vicente de Fora behind. Calçada de São Vicente gives a more intimate shot of the tram descending a cobbled, shaded lane, with balconies and laundry overhead. This is a busy corner. Streets are narrow and traffic and tuk-tuks move through, so step off the tracks only when it is clear. Largo das Portas do Sol is known for pickpockets around the tram boarding point, so keep your bag closed and your belongings close while you shoot.
text.geographic_location: In Alfama, the old hillside district of Lisbon, close to Largo das Portas do Sol and the church of São Vicente de Fora. The Miradouro de Santa Luzia viewpoint is a short walk away.

text.description:
Praça do Comércio is one of Lisbon's biggest squares, 175 by 175 metres, open on one side to the River Tagus. Yellow arcades run along the other three sides, and the Rua Augusta Arch closes the north side. This is where the royal Ribeira Palace stood until the 1755 earthquake. The square was then redesigned as part of the rebuilding of the Baixa. The arch was only finished in the 19th century, and statues on top include Vasco da Gama and the Marquis of Pombal. In the middle stands the bronze statue of King José I, unveiled in 1775.

The square photographs well because everything is symmetrical. The arch sits in the middle, the arcades lead the eye in from both sides, and the statue gives you something in the foreground. The classic shot is from the central line of the square, between the river and the statue, facing north. Use the default lens (1x) for the arch and statue together. Switch to the ultra-wide (0.5x) if you want more of the arcades, and keep your phone level so the straight lines stay straight. Use the telephoto (2x or more) for the statues and clock on top of the arch. If you want a different angle, try the water's edge at the Cais das Colunas, or Rua Augusta looking back at the arch.
text.geographic_location: In the Baixa district, on the Tagus waterfront at the southern end of Rua Augusta. The square lies within the parish of Santa Maria Maior.
text.directions_text: The nearest stop is Terreiro do Paço on the Metro Blue line, about 2 minutes on foot from the phone icon on the map. The square lies to the north-west of the station. The tram stop Praça do Comércio (tram 15E and tram 25E) is also about 2 minutes on foot. From Baixa-Chiado (Metro Blue line and Green line), walk roughly 500 m, about 7 minutes, towards the river; the square lies to the south-east of the station. The phone icon on the map is about 100 m west of the subject. The Navigate buttons below take you straight there.

shooting_on_your_phone.phone_lens: Start with the default lens (1x) for the arch with the statue in front. Use the ultra-wide (0.5x) for the full sweep of arcades. Use the telephoto (2x or more, depending on your phone) for the statues and clock on top of the arch.
shooting_on_your_phone.where_to_stand: Stand about 100 m west of the subject, in Praça do Comércio (the phone icon on the map), and face east. For the classic view, walk to the central line of the square, between the river and the King José I statue, and face north towards the arch. From there the photo shows the arch closing the north side, the bronze statue in the foreground and the yellow arcades on either side.
shooting_on_your_phone.how_to_frame: Turn on the gridlines and put the arch on the centre line so both arcades balance. Keep the statue low in the frame to add depth. For a different view, try the Cais das Colunas at the water's edge, where the two columns can frame the square.
shooting_on_your_phone.phone_settings_tip: Tap on the arch to set focus, then slide the exposure down a little if the sky is bright so the stonework keeps its detail. After dark, the arch is lit, so use night mode and hold the phone steady against your body or a rail.
shooting_on_your_phone.best_time: Late afternoon, when warm side light catches the arch and arcades. The exterior can also be photographed after dark, when it is lit.

text.access_note: The square and the Cais das Colunas are open-air public spaces; if you plan to go up the arch itself, check the official site before you go.
claims_not_in_sources: Keeping the phone level helps keep the straight lines of the arcades from leaning when using the ultra-wide lens.
Bracing the phone against your body or a rail helps keep night shots sharp.

name: Carmo Convent
label: Carmo Convent
camera_source: Researched viewpoint 'Largo do Carmo' (4 web pages); placed at OpenStreetMap 'Largo do Carmo' (way/1356630058): middle (97 m across); moved 5 m off water.
pin_note: Position from OpenStreetMap relation/7524055: the middle of the OpenStreetMap outline 'Convento do Carmo' (149 m across).

text.description:
The Carmo Convent is a Gothic church left roofless by the 1755 Lisbon earthquake. It is now the main trace of that disaster still standing in the old city. The convent was founded in 1389 by Nuno Álvares Pereira, and the church was built in plain Gothic style over the following decades. Today the ruined nave is an archaeological museum, which is why you see sky where the vault used to be.

It photographs well because the story is visible at a glance. The pointed arches between the pillars survived, the stone roof over the nave never came back, and the rose window above the portal is only partly there. From the quiet square in front, the carved doorway and the broken window make a strong subject. The square's fountain adds a foreground that gives the photo some depth.

The phone icon on the map is in Largo do Carmo, in front of the convent entrance. Shooting the outside of the building from there needs no ticket. Start with the whole facade, then move closer for the portal and the rose window. If you go inside, photography is allowed in the ruins, but you will need to hold your phone steady by hand. For a different view, the Elevador de Santa Justa looks down on the open nave and arches, with the Baixa rooftops behind. Any fee for its viewing platform may change, so check on arrival.
text.geographic_location: The convent is in the Chiado neighbourhood, in the civil parish of Santa Maria Maior, on a hill above Rossio square. It faces the castle hill and stands very close to the Santa Justa Lift.
text.directions_text: The nearest Metro station is Baixa-Chiado (Metro Blue line and Green line), about 220 m from the convent, which lies to the north of the station. Rossio (Metro Green line) is a similar short walk away, about 280 m, with the convent to the south-west. If you come by tram, the stops at Figueira Square and Praça da Figueira (tram 12E, tram 15E and tram 25E) are about 240 m away, heading west. The phone icon on the map is about 15 m south-west of the subject. The Navigate buttons below take you straight there.

shooting_on_your_phone.phone_lens: Start with the ultra-wide (0.5x) to fit the whole ruined facade and the fountain in one frame, because the square is fairly close to the building. The default lens (1x) gives a more natural look with less stretching at the edges. Use the telephoto (2x-5x, depending on your phone) for the carved portal and the partly broken rose window.
shooting_on_your_phone.where_to_stand: Stand about 15 m south-west of the subject, in Largo do Carmo (the phone icon on the map), and face north-east. From here you can see the Gothic ruined facade and the entrance, with the square and its fountain in the foreground. The middle of the building lies a little to the north-east of this spot. The elevated view from the Elevador de Santa Justa is the alternative, if you want to look down on the open nave.
shooting_on_your_phone.how_to_frame: Turn on the gridlines and keep the vertical lines of the facade straight, so the building does not seem to lean. Place the fountain low in the frame and let the doorway and rose window fill the upper part. Then take a second, closer shot of the portal's carved arches. If you go up to the Elevador de Santa Justa, aim down at the nave so the row of arches leads the eye towards the rooftops.
shooting_on_your_phone.phone_settings_tip: Tap on the facade to set focus, then drag the exposure slider down slightly so the pale stone keeps its detail and the sky behind the broken window does not wash out. Portrait mode is not needed here; the building looks better in a normal photo.
shooting_on_your_phone.best_time: Go earlier in the day if you can, when the square is likely to be quieter and easier to photograph without people in front of the entrance.

text.access_note: The square in front is an open public space, but the ruins are a museum, so check the official site before you go for visiting details.
claims_not_in_sources: The square is likely to be quieter earlier in the day.
A slightly lower exposure helps keep detail in pale stone against a bright sky.

name: Cristo Rei
label: Cristo Rei
camera_source: Researched viewpoint 'Santuário Nacional de Cristo Rei' (4 web pages); placed at at the subject (split pin).
pin_note: Position from OpenStreetMap way/87891338: the middle of the OpenStreetMap outline 'National Shrine of Christ the King' (35 m across).

text.description: Cristo Rei is a huge statue of Christ with arms stretched wide, standing on the south bank of the Tagus in Almada and facing across the water towards Lisbon. The sanctuary was inaugurated on 17 May 1959, and the idea came from the Christ the Redeemer statue in Rio de Janeiro. The figure is about 28 metres tall and stands on a pedestal of about 82 metres, built as four arches, on a clifftop plateau high above the river. It is the highest point in Almada. That scale is why it photographs so well. From the foot of the pedestal you look straight up at the open arms against the sky, with the concrete arches and the gardens in the foreground. Several guides say this is the best view of the statue itself, because it is too big to frame properly from the viewing platform at the top. Stand at the phone icon on the map, step back as far as the esplanade allows, and tilt the phone upwards. Keep the phone level and straight, or the pedestal will lean. If you also want the bridge and the city, the Cais das Colunas in Lisbon and the Miradouro do Bairro do Alvito show Cristo Rei far across the river with the 25 de Abril Bridge. The statue looks small from there, so zoom in or frame it wide.
text.geographic_location: Cristo Rei is in Almada, on the south bank of the Tagus directly across the river from Lisbon, on a clifftop plateau overlooking the Tagus, with the 25 de Abril Bridge nearby. It looks over the city rather than standing inside it.
text.directions_text: From Lisbon you can cross the Tagus by the Cacilheiro ferry to Cacilhas in Almada, or take a train to Pragal station, then continue to the sanctuary. The sanctuary can also be reached by car over the 25 de Abril Bridge. Once you are at the sanctuary, the phone icon on the map is at the foot of the pedestal, so you do not need to walk any further. The phone icon on the map is at the subject itself. The Navigate buttons below take you straight there.

shooting_on_your_phone.phone_lens: Use the ultra-wide (0.5x) close to the base to fit the pedestal and statue together while looking up. Step back and use the default lens (1x) for a calmer, less stretched view. Use the telephoto (2x-5x, depending on your phone) for details such as the arms and the face of the statue, or if you shoot Cristo Rei from across the river.
shooting_on_your_phone.where_to_stand: Stand right at the subject: the phone icon on the map marks the spot. Stand on Santuário Nacional de Cristo Rei, on the esplanade and ground level at the foot of the pedestal, looking up at the statue. From here you see the open-armed statue from below against the sky, with the concrete pedestal and the gardens in the foreground.
shooting_on_your_phone.how_to_frame: Turn on the gridlines and line the statue up on the centre line so the pedestal stays straight. Include a little of the gardens or the arches at the bottom of the frame to show how tall it is. Take one wide shot, then one closer shot of the figure. If you want the bridge in the picture too, the Cais das Colunas or the Miradouro do Bairro do Alvito in Lisbon show Cristo Rei across the river as an alternative.
shooting_on_your_phone.phone_settings_tip: Tap the statue to focus, then slide the exposure down a little so the sky stays blue and the figure does not turn into a dark shape. Portrait mode is not useful here. Hold the phone steady with both hands.
shooting_on_your_phone.best_time: Choose a clear day, when the statue stands out against a blue sky. Gentle evening light also suits the stone, but check the closing time first, since the sanctuary may close near sunset in winter.

text.access_note: The ground level and esplanade at the foot of the statue are free to enter, but the lift to the viewing platform is ticketed and may not always run, so check the official site (cristorei.pt) before you go.
claims_not_in_sources: A clear blue sky makes the statue stand out more in photos.
Lowering the exposure slider helps keep the sky blue and the statue detailed when shooting upwards.
Gentle evening light flatters the stone of the statue.
Tilting a phone upwards from close to the base can make the pedestal look as if it is leaning.

name: 25 de Abril Bridge
label: 25 de Abril Bridge
camera_source: Researched viewpoint 'Santuário de Cristo Rei' (3 web pages); placed at OpenStreetMap 'Santuário Nacional de Cristo Rei' (way/87891338): middle (35 m across); moved 10 m off buildings.
pin_note: Position from OpenStreetMap way/485215103: large area '25th of April Bridge' (3205 m across): previous pin kept, it lies inside.

text.description:
The 25 de Abril Bridge links Lisbon with Almada on the south bank of the Tagus. Its main span is 1,013 metres long, and it opened on 6 August 1966 as the Salazar Bridge. After the Carnation Revolution of 1974 it was renamed for the date of the revolution. The upper deck carries six lanes of traffic, and a double-track railway has run on the lower deck since 1999.

The best-known view is from the observation deck at the feet of the Cristo Rei statue, on the south bank. From up there the whole bridge stretches across the river with the Lisbon skyline behind it. The river gives you plenty of open space, and the long line of the roadway leads the eye towards the city. The bridge's southern end was planned right beside the Cristo Rei monument, so the two sit close together.

For a second angle, try Doca de Santo Amaro on the Lisbon side. There the steelwork rises overhead, with boat masts in front and the towers against the sky. Largo das Necessidades gives a wider view across the river, framed by the pink palace and church. Phone photos from any of these places work best with the bridge placed off-centre and a patch of sky or water left around it.
text.geographic_location: The bridge crosses the Tagus between Lisbon on the north bank and Almada on the south bank.
text.directions_text: This viewpoint is across the river in Almada, so allow time to cross the Tagus. The viewpoint is the Santuário de Cristo Rei in Almada, on the south bank of the Tagus, so check the official site or a map for how to get there. From the phone icon on the map, the bridge lies to the north. Check the official site before you go for how to reach the top deck. The phone icon on the map is about 1.3 km south of the subject. The Navigate buttons below take you straight there.

shooting_on_your_phone.phone_lens: Start with the default lens (1x) to take in the bridge, the river and the skyline together. Use ultra-wide (0.5x) if you want more of the deck and sky in the frame, and telephoto (2x-5x, depending on your phone) to pick out the towers and the city behind them.
shooting_on_your_phone.where_to_stand: Stand about 1.3 km south of the subject, at Santuário de Cristo Rei (the phone icon on the map), and face north. From there the bridge stretches across the Tagus to the north, with the Lisbon skyline behind it. This is the classic postcard view of the bridge and the city. As an alternative, a free path down the hillside from the sanctuary is said to give a view of the bridge too.
shooting_on_your_phone.how_to_frame: Turn on gridlines and line the roadway up with a horizontal line so the bridge doesn't tilt. Place the bridge along the lower third and let the skyline and sky fill the rest. For a different angle, Doca de Santo Amaro on the Lisbon side gives a close-up with the steelwork overhead and boat masts in front.
shooting_on_your_phone.phone_settings_tip: Tap on the bridge or the city to set focus, then slide the exposure down a little so the sky keeps its colour at sunset. Try panorama mode for the full sweep of the river, moving slowly and steadily. After dark, use night mode and rest your elbows on a rail or wall to keep still.
shooting_on_your_phone.best_time: Golden hour or sunset.

text.access_note: The top deck at Cristo Rei is reached by a paid lift, so check the official site before you go for opening times and ticket details.

name: MAAT
label: MAAT
camera_source: Researched viewpoint 'Avenida Brasília' (3 web pages); placed at OpenStreetMap 'Avenida de Brasília' (way/429797068): point nearest the subject (517 m long).
pin_note: Position from OpenStreetMap relation/11381632: the middle of the OpenStreetMap outline 'Museum of Art, Architecture and Technology' (220 m across).

text.description: MAAT is a museum of art, architecture and technology on the River Tagus, west of the city centre. The newer building, designed by Amanda Levete Architects, is a low, curving shape covered in ceramic tiles, and it sits beside the older Tejo Power Station, one of Portugal's best-known industrial buildings from the first half of the 20th century. The museum's programme began on 30 June 2016, and the new building opened to the public on 5 October 2016. It photographs well because the curves, the tile texture and the open river setting all fit into one frame. From the riverside promenade in front, you can show the tiled facade and its curves with the river and the bridge behind. A second option is the wave-shaped white roof in the foreground, with the Tagus, the 25 de Abril Bridge and the Belém riverfront beyond. For the facade, walk a little way back from the building so the whole curve fits without tilting your phone upwards. Tap the brightest tiles to set focus and exposure, then lower the exposure slightly if the sky washes out. Some temporary exhibitions restrict photography indoors, so keep your main pictures outside.
text.geographic_location: MAAT is on the Tagus waterfront in the west of Lisbon, next to the old Tejo Power Station. The riverside promenade runs along the front of the building.
text.directions_text: From the Altinho (MAAT) tram stop on tram 15E, the building is to the south-east, about 3 minutes on foot. From the Rua Pinto Ferreira tram stop, also tram 15E, it is to the south-west, about 5 minutes on foot. For the quieter stretch of promenade, walk east from the ferry terminal along the river. The phone icon on the map is about 15 m north of the subject. The Navigate buttons below take you straight there.

shooting_on_your_phone.phone_lens: Use the default lens (1x) from the promenade to fit the facade with the river and bridge behind it. Switch to the ultra-wide (0.5x) if you are close and want the full curve. Use the telephoto (2x or more, depending on your phone) for close-ups of the tile pattern.
shooting_on_your_phone.where_to_stand: Stand about 15 m north of the subject, on Avenida Brasília (the phone icon on the map), and face south. This is the riverside promenade in front of the facade, set well back from the building, which lies to the south of you. From here you see the ceramic tile facade and its curves framed against the river and the bridge.
shooting_on_your_phone.how_to_frame: Turn on gridlines and keep the horizon level, with the building's curve running across the lower half and the river and bridge above. If you want a second view, the wave-shaped white roof of MAAT shows the Tagus, the 25 de Abril Bridge and the Belém riverfront behind it. The bridge has no pedestrian access, so do not plan to shoot from it.
shooting_on_your_phone.phone_settings_tip: Tap the tiles to set focus, then drag the exposure slider down a little so the white surfaces keep their detail. Take a few frames as people walk past, or try a Live Photo.
shooting_on_your_phone.best_time: Morning or late afternoon. Midday sun flattens the texture of the tiles.

text.access_note: The promenade in front of the building is an open outdoor space, but entry to the museum and its roof may need a ticket or may be restricted, so check the official site before you go.
claims_not_in_sources: The promenade in front of the building is an open outdoor public space.
Gridlines help keep the horizon level when photographing curved buildings.
Entry to the museum building and rooftop may be ticketed or restricted on some days.

name: National Pantheon (Santa Engrácia)
label: National Pantheon
camera_source: Researched viewpoint 'Campo de Santa Clara' (2 web pages); placed at OpenStreetMap 'Campo de Santa Clara' (way/9252469): point nearest the subject (186 m long).
pin_note: Position from OpenStreetMap way/9253917: the middle of the OpenStreetMap outline 'Panteão Nacional' (91 m across).

text.description:
The National Pantheon is the white, domed building in Alfama. It began as the Church of Santa Engrácia. Work on the present building started in 1681 to a design by the royal architect João Antunes, but it dragged on for so long that "the works of Santa Engrácia" became a Portuguese saying for a job that never ends. The dome was only added in the 20th century, and the building was reinaugurated in 1966. It had already become the National Pantheon in 1916, and today it holds the tombs of well-known Portuguese figures, including the fado singer Amália Rodrigues and the footballer Eusébio.

It photographs well because of its shape. The plan is a Greek cross, the façades curve in and out in the baroque manner, and the pale stone stands out against the sky. For the exterior, use the phone icon on the map, where the façade and dome sit one above the other. If you can, keep the building centred so the two sides match. Check the area before you plan your shot: on Tuesdays and Saturdays the flea market fills Campo de Santa Clara and can block the view. For a different angle, the pantheon can be seen across the garden at Jardim Botto Machado. It also shows as a dome in the background from Miradouro de Santa Luzia, over the Alfama rooftops.
text.geographic_location: In the Alfama district of Lisbon, close to the Monastery of São Vicente de Fora and a short walk up from the Santa Apolónia area by the river.
text.directions_text: Take the Metro Blue line to Santa Apolónia; the pantheon is about 240 m from the station, to the north-west, so walk north-west up into the Alfama streets. Alternatively, ride tram 28E to Voz do Operário (353 m away) and walk east to the pantheon, or get off at Calçada de São Vicente (386 m away) and walk north-east. Both are a short walk. The phone icon on the map is about 80 m north of the subject. The Navigate buttons below take you straight there.

shooting_on_your_phone.phone_lens: Start with the default lens (1x) from where you stand. Switch to the ultra-wide (0.5x) if you are close and want the whole façade and dome in one frame. Use telephoto (2x-5x, depending on your phone) for the dome and the carved details.
shooting_on_your_phone.where_to_stand: Stand about 80 m north of the subject, in Campo de Santa Clara (the phone icon on the map), and face south. From here the white façade and dome can be framed together. Standing directly in front of the dome gives the most symmetrical frame.
shooting_on_your_phone.how_to_frame: Switch on gridlines and line the dome up with the centre line so both sides of the building match. Keep your phone upright and level to avoid the walls leaning inwards, especially with the ultra-wide lens. Leave a little sky above the dome. For a different view, try the pantheon across the garden at Jardim Botto Machado, or the dome among the Alfama rooftops from Miradouro de Santa Luzia.
shooting_on_your_phone.phone_settings_tip: Tap the white stonework to set focus, then slide the exposure down a touch so the façade keeps its detail against the bright sky. If the sky looks flat, tap on the sky instead and check the stone still looks right.
shooting_on_your_phone.best_time: Morning or late afternoon is usually kinder to pale stone than harsh midday sun. Go on a day other than Tuesday or Saturday if you want the area clear of market stalls.

text.access_note: The area outside is open public space, but the pantheon is a national monument and its dome terrace is reported to be ticketed, so check the official site for current details before you go.
claims_not_in_sources: Morning or late afternoon light is usually softer and more flattering on pale stone than midday sun.
The dome terrace is reported to be ticketed (from a single blog).
